files.README.md:
# Wave Arena: firing cooldowns and scheduled enemies (c)

Implement arena_step: a/d move horizontally (clamped to columns 0..8), f fires, and . waits. Every action is one fixed simulation tick (250 ms). First reduce a positive cooldown by one; fire only when it is zero, then set it to 3. A shot removes the nearest enemy in the player column and awards one point. Next move surviving enemies down one row; reaching row 4 costs one health and removes the enemy. Increment tick, then spawn at ticks 4,8,12,... in columns 4,2,6 repeating, at row 0. Win at three points while alive; zero health loses. Finished state stays unchanged. The terminal game and replay producer both call your callback.

Edit `mechanics.c`. `model.h` defines the fixed-size state; it owns its arrays, and callbacks borrow a mutable pointer/reference to it. No heap-owned gameplay buffers are returned. The main program calls your mechanics for every input; it does not implement a second version of the game.

Build: `cc -std=c17 mechanics.c main.c -o game`
Play: `./game` (press Enter after each action; q exits).
Tests: `cc -std=c17 mechanics.c tests.c -o project-tests && ./project-tests`
Replay: `./game --replay ....faa.fddddf > replay.ndjson`

Replay files contain a header followed by native-computed JSON frames. Import replay.ndjson on the project page; its viewer displays those frames without simulating movement, cooldowns or enemies.

Requirements: a C17 compiler. Windows: executable names may end in .exe; use game.exe/project-tests.exe instead of ./game/./project-tests.

The starter compiles and deliberately fails named tests. Implement the mechanics, run tests, then play and export your own replay. The reference and explanation stay on the website; the starter download does not replace your work with the solution.

explanation: Update order matters: player movement, cooldown decrement, optional shot, enemy movement/damage, tick increment, scheduled spawn, win check. The nearest target is the enemy with the greatest row in the player column. Remove it before advancing enemies so a successful shot prevents that enemy from reaching the player row. Shift remaining enemies when removing to preserve deterministic ordering. Spawning after movement keeps a new enemy at row zero for its first exported frame. Both interactive play and --replay call this same learner function; there is no browser copy of the rules.
